claim: Mice were trained to perform an audiovisual (AV) rule-switching task where they made decisions using auditory stimuli while ignoring simultaneously presented visual stimuli or vice versa.
source: We trained mice to perform an AV rule-switching task, in which they made decisions using auditory stimuli while ignoring simultaneously presented visual stimuli or vice versa.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: Trial presentation was self-paced in a virtual foraging environment wherein a visual track was advanced by forward locomotion on a spherical treadmill.
source: Trial presentation was self-paced in a virtual foraging environment wherein a visual track was advanced by forward locomotion on a spherical treadmill (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental setup and references Figure 1A showing the apparatus.

claim: A task-irrelevant random double sweep (RDS) sound was presented during inter-trial intervals (ITIs) for mapping auditory receptive fields in each attentional state.
source: A task-irrelevant random double sweep (RDS) sound was presented during inter-trial intervals (ITIs) for mapping auditory receptive fields in each attentional state (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental protocol and references Figure 1B.

claim: Decision stimuli consisted of 1 s auditory tone clouds (TCs; centered at 8 or 17 kHz) and/or visual drifting gratings (horizontal or vertical orientation).
source: Decision stimuli were presented after variable track length, consisting of 1 s auditory tone clouds (TCs; centered at 8 or 17 kHz) and/or visual drifting gratings (horizontal or vertical orientation; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus properties used in the experiment.

claim: Lick responses following targets produced water rewards and lick responses following distractors produced dark timeouts.
source: Lick responses following targets (hits) and distractors (false alarms [FAs]) produced water rewards and dark timeouts, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral contingencies of the task.

claim: Each session began with a block of unimodal decision stimuli, which cued the attended modality of a subsequent AV block.
source: Each session began with a block of unimodal decision stimuli, which cued the attended modality of a subsequent AV block (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the task structure and references Figure 1D.

claim: Decision stimuli had identical physical properties but different behavioral significance between rules.
source: Decision stimuli had identical physical properties but different behavioral significance between rules (e.g., licks following ARVU were rewarded in A-rule but punished in V-rule).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design to isolate attentional effects.

claim: Block sequences (A-rule then V-rule, or vice versa) were counterbalanced across sessions.
source: Block sequences (A-rule then V-rule, or vice versa) were also counterbalanced across sessions (Figure 1D.c).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design to control for order effects.

claim: Analysis was restricted to sessions in which discrimination was well above chance (d'>1.5) for both rules.
source: We used two approaches to ensure that animals were engaged during both task rules. First, we restricted analysis to sessions in which discrimination was well above chance (d'>1.5) for both rules, and for which FA rates were below 0.5 for the stimuli with reward valences that conflicted across rules (AUVR in the A-rule, ARVU in the V-rule; Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the inclusion criteria for behavioral sessions.

claim: Pupil size was measured in a subset of sessions (n=14 sessions, 5 mice) as a correlate of arousal and behavioral performance.
source: Second, for a subset of sessions (n=14 sessions, 5 mice) we measured pupil size, a well-established correlate of arousal and behavioral performance (Bradley et al., 2008; McGinley et al., 2015; Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript describes the measurement approach and cites supporting literature.

claim: Pupil size is a well-established correlate of arousal and behavioral performance.
source: Second, for a subset of sessions (n=14 sessions, 5 mice) we measured pupil size, a well-established correlate of arousal and behavioral performance (Bradley et al., 2008; McGinley et al., 2015; Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies establishing this relationship.

claim: No difference in pupil size was observed between rules during bimodal blocks.
source: No difference in pupil size was observed between rules during bimodal blocks (Figure 2C; A-rule bimodal: 0.29±0.05 norm. diameter ± SD, V-rule bimodal: 0.30±0.05; Z=–1.0, p=0.30, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank [WSR], Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted p-values).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of pupil size measurements across conditions.

claim: Pupil diameters were significantly larger during the bimodal portion of the task compared to the auditory-only unimodal portion of the task.
source: As expected, pupil diameters were significantly larger during the bimodal portion of the task, when visual stimuli were present and the task had increased in difficulty, compared to the auditory-only unimodal portion of the task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; A-rule unimodal: 0.28±0.04, A-rule bimodal: 0.29±0.05; Z=–2.6, p=0.009).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing pupil size across task segments.

claim: Differences in locomotion speed were not observed between rules.
source: Differences in locomotion speed were also not observed between rules (all p≥0.623; all |Z|≤1.29, paired WSR).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of locomotion measurements.

claim: Arousal and motor activity were comparable between rules, suggesting that differences in neuronal activity may be attributable to modality-selective attention.
source: Arousal and motor activity were thus comparable between rules, suggesting that differences in neuronal activity may be attributable to modality-selective attention.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the pupil and locomotion data.

claim: In total, 742 single units (SUs) were recorded from AC activity in 10 mice during 23 behavioral sessions meeting inclusion criteria.
source: In total, we recorded AC activity in 10 mice during 23 behavioral sessions meeting inclusion criteria.
evidence: The manuscript reports the sample size for the study.

claim: The putative cortical depth of each sorted single unit was assigned by calculating the fractional position of the channel with the largest waveform amplitude within the span of channels in AC.
source: The putative cortical depth of each sorted single unit (SU) was assigned by calculating the fractional position of the channel with the largest waveform amplitude within the span of channels in AC, as estimated from spontaneous and tone-evoked recordings following the task (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for depth estimation.

claim: A separate set of experiments to visualize probe tracks with the fluorescent dye Di-I provided support for the depth estimation technique.
source: A separate set of experiments to visualize probe tracks with the fluorescent dye Di-I provided support for this depth estimation technique (Figure 3C; DiCarlo et al., 1996; Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes histological validation of the depth estimation method.

claim: Single units were divided into superficial, middle, and deep groups, approximating the supragranular, granular, and infragranular laminae.
source: We then divided the fractional depth values into superficial, middle, and deep groups, approximating the supragranular, granular, and infragranular laminae.
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification scheme for cortical depth.

claim: Single units were further divided into narrow-spiking (NS, putative inhibitory; n=130, 18%) and broad-spiking (BS, predominantly excitatory; n=612, 82%) populations based on trough-peak time.
source: We further divided SUs into narrow-spiking (NS, putative inhibitory; n=130, 18%) and broad-spiking (BS, predominantly excitatory; n=612, 82%) populations based on trough-peak time (Figure 3D; Bigelow et al., 2019; Cardin et al., 2007; Nandy et al., 2017; Phillips et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification method and cites supporting literature.

claim: Activity patterns evoked by decision stimuli and modulatory effects of task rule were diverse.
source: Activity patterns evoked by decision stimuli and modulatory effects of task rule were diverse (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observed neural responses and references example data.

claim: Mean firing rates (FRs) were measured during the first 300 ms post-stimulus onset to capture a predominantly sensory-driven response component.
source: To capture a predominantly sensory-driven response component, we measured mean firing rates (FRs) during the first 300 ms post-stimulus onset (Figure 4B), which preceded most lick responses (lick latency median: 611 ms; 5–95th percentiles: 289–1078 ms; 5.4% of licks <300 ms, n=2852 total lick trials across dataset).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis window and provides supporting behavioral data.

claim: Responses in the deep layers to AR* stimuli were suppressed in the A-rule relative to the V-rule for both NS and BS units.
source: Averaging across units, responses in the deep layers were suppressed in the A-rule relative to the V-rule for both NS and BS units (Figure 4C; deep BS: p=2.8e-4, Z=4.1, median fold change [FC; A-rule/V-rule]: 0.89, n=333 SUs; deep NS: p=0.011, Z=2.9, median FC: 0.87, n=66; paired WSR, FDR-adjusted p-values; see Figure 4—source data 1A for full stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of firing rate responses.

claim: No significant group-level change in firing rate was found in middle or superficial units in response to AR* stimuli.
source: No significant group-level change was found in middle or superficial units.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of significant effects in these populations.

claim: Individual units with significant FR decreases in the A-rule substantially outnumbered units with significant FR increases for all unit populations other than superficial and mid-depth BS units.
source: Consistent with group-level trends, individual units with significant FR decreases in the A-rule (p<0.01, unpaired t-test) substantially outnumbered units with significant FR increases for all unit populations other than superficial and mid-depth BS units (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of individual unit modulation patterns.

claim: Deep BS units showed suppressed firing rates in the A-rule in response to AU* stimuli.
source: At the group level, superficial and middle unit responses did not differ significantly between conditions, whereas deep BS units were suppressed in the A-rule (Figure 4D; deep BS: p=2.0e-06, Z=5.11, median FC: 0.81, n=321; paired WSR, FDR-adjusted p-values; see Figure 4—source data 1B for full stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of firing rate responses to AU* stimuli.

claim: Most units showed the same direction of modulation for AR* and AU* stimuli.
source: We further found that most units showed the same direction of modulation for AR* and AU* stimuli (Figure 4E), with a similar modulation sign observed for 78% of BS units (50% suppressed for both AR* and AU*, 28% enhanced for both) and 99% of NS units (68% suppressed for both, 31% enhanced for both).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis comparing modulation patterns across stimulus types.

claim: Modality-selective attention similarly influences firing rates evoked by task-relevant target and distractor sounds with different acoustic properties and learned behavioral values.
source: These findings suggest that modality-selective attention similarly influences FRs evoked by task-relevant target and distractor sounds with different acoustic properties and learned behavioral values.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the consistency of modulation across stimulus types.

claim: Middle- and deep-layer BS and NS populations exhibited group-level FR suppression during the A-rule in response to task-irrelevant RDS sounds.
source: Using the same analysis window (300 ms post-stimulus onset, Figure 4F), we found that attention-related modulation of FR responses evoked by task-irrelevant sounds was highly similar to that observed for both types of decision stimuli: middle- and deep-layer BS and NS populations exhibited group-level FR suppression during the A-rule (Figure 4G), whereas superficial layer units showed no difference (middle BS: p=6.0e-3, Z=3.1, median FC: 0.85, n=112; middle NS: p=0.014, Z=2.7, median FC: 0.65, n=28; deep BS: p=1.2e-6, Z=5.2, median FC: 0.84, n=309; deep NS: p=0.021, Z=2.5, median FC: 0.80, n=64; paired WSR; see Figure 4—source data 2 for full stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of responses to task-irrelevant sounds.

claim: Auditory-selective attention tends to reduce FR responses to sounds, regardless of their behavioral relevance, valence, or spectral content, and these influences are strongest for deep-layer units.
source: Together, these results show that auditory-selective attention tends to reduce FR responses to sounds, regardless of their behavioral relevance, valence, or spectral content, and that these influences are strongest for deep-layer units.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings across different sound types and cortical depths.

claim: Modulation of ongoing activity in sensory cortex can influence subsequent sensory-evoked responses.
source: Previous studies have found that modulation of ongoing activity in sensory cortex can influence subsequent sensory-evoked responses (Arieli et al., 1996; Haider and McCormick, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies establishing this relationship.

claim: Significant group-level decreases in pre-stimulus FRs during the A-rule were observed for units in the middle NS and deep BS groups.
source: We observed significant group-level decreases in pre-stimulus FRs during the A-rule for units in the middle NS and deep BS groups, but no modulation of superficial units (Figure 5B; middle NS: p=0.039, Z=2.48, median FC: 0.71, n=28; deep BS: p=4.2e-05, Z=4.49, median FC: 0.87, n=336; paired WSR, FDR-adjusted p-values; see Figure 5—source data 1 for full stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of pre-stimulus firing rates.

claim: After normalizing evoked firing rates by pre-stimulus firing rates, the middle- and deep-layer unit population responses no longer differed between rules.
source: Following this adjustment and after FDR correction, the middle- and deep-layer unit population responses no longer differed between rules (Figure 5C; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of normalized firing rate analysis.

claim: Group-level decreases in evoked FRs during A-rule are largely due to generalized suppression of ongoing AC activity.
source: Together, these results suggest that group-level decreases in evoked FRs during A-rule are largely due to generalized suppression of ongoing AC activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the pre-stimulus and normalized firing rate analyses.

claim: The RDS mapping stimulus was used to generate spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) through reverse correlation.
source: The RDS mapping stimulus, which we have previously used to efficiently identify auditory response properties and AV interactions (Bigelow et al., 2022), was used to generate spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) through reverse correlation (Figure 6A; Aertsen and Johannesma, 1981; de Boer, 1968; Gourévitch et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis method and cites supporting literature.

claim: Units were divided into those with tuned STRFs (n=172) and those without feature-evoked changes (untuned, n=409).
source: Tuning for each STRF was measured through a trial-to-trial reliability metric, which we used to divide units into those with activity changes that were reliably evoked by defined spectral or temporal features (tuned STRFs, n=172; Figure 6C.a) and those without feature-evoked changes (untuned, n=409; Figure 6C.b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification method and reports sample sizes.

claim: Spiking activity levels were higher in tuned units compared to untuned.
source: Spiking activity levels were higher in tuned units compared to untuned (Figure 6D.a).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of activity levels between groups.

claim: Responses to AR*, AU*, and RDS stimuli were significantly modulated by task rule in the untuned group, but not the tuned group.
source: We then examined attentional modulation of stimulus responses between the tuned and subsampled untuned groups. Responses to the rewarded TC (AR*), unrewarded TC (AU*), and the RDS mapping stimuli were significantly modulated by task rule in the untuned group, but not the tuned group (tuned: all p≥0.18, all |Z|≤1.72; untuned: all p≤0.023, all |Z|≥2.27; one-way WSR vs. modulation of 1 [equal across rules], FDR-adjusted p-values; Figure 6—source data 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing modulation between tuned and untuned groups.

claim: Group-level suppression during auditory attention is driven by units that do not exhibit strong tuning preferences.
source: An important caveat is that the RDS stimuli may not capture all units with some degree of tuning preference. As such, a conservative interpretation would be that group-level suppression during auditory attention is driven by units that do not exhibit strong tuning preferences.
evidence: The manuscript provides a cautious interpretation of the tuning analysis results.

claim: Both tuned and untuned populations contained units with significant evoked responses to the two TCs, although fractions of responsive units were higher in the tuned group.
source: Additionally, both tuned and untuned populations contained units with significant evoked responses to the two TCs, although fractions of responsive units were higher in the tuned group (Figure 6D.c).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of stimulus responsiveness between groups.

claim: An absence of STRF tuning does not imply that units were not responsive to the task stimuli.
source: This shows that an absence of STRF tuning does not imply that units were not responsive to the task stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the responsiveness analysis.

claim: There was a strong BF preference for a 1-octave band around the center frequency of the rewarded TC.
source: Consistent with previous work showing that task demands shape frequency representation in AC (Atiani et al., 2009; Fritz et al., 2005; Fritz et al., 2003; Yin et al., 2014), we found a strong BF preference for a 1-octave band around the center frequency of the rewarded TC (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of best frequency distributions and cites supporting literature.

claim: Distributions of BFs measured during the A-rule and V-rule were strikingly similar.
source: Furthermore, distributions of BFs measured during the A-rule and V-rule were strikingly similar.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of BF distributions across rules.

claim: In this task, AC had shifted its frequency representation in a manner that was not rule-dependent.
source: This suggests that in our task, AC had shifted its frequency representation in a manner that was not rule-dependent.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the similarity of BF distributions across rules.

claim: No difference in modulation by rule was observed between units grouped by their BF for responses to AR* or AU* TCs.
source: No difference between the tuning groups was observed for responses to AR* or AU* TCs (Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric ANOVA, all p>0.12, all H<5.5, FDR-adjusted p-values; Figure 6—source data 1C, D), suggesting that frequency tuning does not determine suppression or enhancement by attention in this task.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing modulation across BF groups.

claim: Frequency tuning does not determine suppression or enhancement by attention in this task.
source: No difference between the tuning groups was observed for responses to AR* or AU* TCs (Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric ANOVA, all p>0.12, all H<5.5, FDR-adjusted p-values; Figure 6—source data 1C, D), suggesting that frequency tuning does not determine suppression or enhancement by attention in this task.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the lack of BF-dependent modulation.

claim: FR changes do not necessarily imply changes in the amount of information spikes carry about sensory stimuli.
source: Previous work has established that FR changes do not necessarily imply changes in the amount of information spikes carry about sensory stimuli.
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge from previous work.

claim: Optogenetic activation of inhibitory interneurons can reduce FRs in AC without changing information, suggesting increased encoding efficiency.
source: For instance, optogenetic activation of inhibitory interneurons can reduce FRs in AC without changing information, suggesting increased encoding efficiency (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study demonstrating this phenomenon.

claim: Locomotion reduces both FRs and information in AC.
source: By contrast, locomotion reduces both FRs and information in AC (Bigelow et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study demonstrating this effect.

claim: A PSTH-based neural pattern decoder was used to compare sound discrimination across attentional states.
source: To determine whether reduced FRs evoked by decision stimuli were accompanied by changes in information or encoding efficiency, we used a peristimulus time histogram (PSTH)-based neural pattern decoder to compare sound discrimination across attentional states (Foffani and Moxon, 2004; Hoglen et al., 2018; Malone et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis method and cites supporting literature.

claim: A 0–300 ms post-stimulus onset window was used for decoding analysis to restrict decoding to a predominantly sensory-driven component of the response.
source: As in previous analyses, a 0–300 ms post-stimulus onset window was used in this method to restrict decoding to a predominantly sensory-driven component of the response.
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis window selection.

claim: Task rule could be decoded at greater than chance levels from responses to all four AV stimuli, and at all depth and NS/BS groups.
source: We found that task rule could be decoded at greater than chance levels from responses to all four AV stimuli, and at all depth and NS/BS groups, showing that attentional state modulates decision stimulus PSTH responses throughout AC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding analysis results.

claim: Attentional state modulates decision stimulus PSTH responses throughout AC.
source: We found that task rule could be decoded at greater than chance levels from responses to all four AV stimuli, and at all depth and NS/BS groups, showing that attentional state modulates decision stimulus PSTH responses throughout AC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the decoding results.

claim: Classification accuracy for the auditory decision stimuli (AR*, AU*) was higher than chance for all depth and BS/NS groups in both rules.
source: In both rules, classification accuracy for the auditory decision stimuli (AR*, AU*) was higher than chance for all depth and BS/NS groups (see scatter plots in Figure 7B; all p≤1.4e-05, all |Z|≥4.2, one-way WSR vs. chance [50%]; see Figure 7—source data 2A for stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of decoding accuracy.

claim: Sound classification accuracy (AR*, AU*) did not significantly differ across the A-rule and V-rule.
source: Sound classification accuracy (AR*, AU*) did not significantly differ across the A-rule and V-rule (Figure 7B, AR* vs. AU* comparison across rules: all p≥0.17, all |Z|≤1.39, see Figure 7—source data 3A for full stats; paired WSR on decoder accuracy in A-rule vs. V-rule by depth and NS/BS groups).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing decoding accuracy across rules.

claim: Despite a reduction in activity levels during auditory attention, there was no loss in decoder accuracy, suggesting a possible change in encoding efficiency.
source: Despite a reduction in activity levels during auditory attention, there was no loss in decoder accuracy, suggesting a possible change in encoding efficiency.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the decoding and firing rate results.

claim: Classifier accuracy and raw information were correlated with FR.
source: Through analysis of all decoder runs, we found that classifier accuracy and raw information were indeed correlated with FR (accuracy: r(3001)=0.49, p=2.3e-180; MI: r(3001)=0.41, p=1.5e-123; Pearson's correlation, all AR* vs. AU* decoder runs).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results.

claim: Encoding efficiency (bits/spike) increased by ~20% during the A-rule for deep-layer BS units.
source: We found that this encoding efficiency measure increased by ~20% during the A-rule for deep-layer BS units (Figure 7C, AR* vs. AU* comparison across rules: deep BS: p=2.9e-04, Z=–4.06, paired WSR, FDR-adjusted p-value; median FC: 1.19 [fold change: A-rule/V-rule]; V-rule: 0.15±0.13, A-rule: 0.19±0.19, mean bits/spike ± SDs, n=233; all other groups p≥0.40, all |Z|≤1.47; see Figure 7—source data 4A for full stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of encoding efficiency.

claim: No other unit subpopulations showed significant changes in encoding efficiency.
source: No other unit subpopulations showed significant changes.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of significant effects in other populations.

claim: Visual stimulus identity does not contribute substantially to decoder accuracy or encoding efficiency at the level of group analysis.
source: Analysis of these comparisons separately yields highly similar results (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Figure 7—source data 2–4), suggesting that visual stimulus identity does not contribute substantially to decoder accuracy or encoding efficiency at the level of group analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis comparing results with visual stimuli separated and draws an inference.

claim: Encoding efficiency showed a significant A-rule increase in the deep BS subpopulation for STRF-spike train MI.
source: No differences in encoding efficiency between conditions were observed in the superficial or middle BS/NS groups, or the deep NS group. Instead, consistent with our earlier findings for decision stimuli, encoding efficiency showed a significant A-rule increase in the deep BS subpopulation (Figure 7F; deep BS: p=0.014, Z=–3.05, median FC: 1.25, n=50; paired WSR, FDR-adjusted p-value; FC: A-rule/V-rule; mean bits/spike ± SDs; all other groups p≥0.24, all |Z|≤1.66; see Figure 7—source data 5 for full stats).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of STRF-based encoding efficiency.

claim: During auditory attention, stimulus encoding is better described by a linear STRF filter and thus better tracks physical sound features.
source: This finding shows that during auditory attention, stimulus encoding is better described by a linear STRF filter and thus better tracks physical sound features.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the STRF-based encoding efficiency results.

claim: Increased encoding efficiency resulting from decreased spiking is a general effect of auditory attention in deep-layer BS units, regardless of the context-based behavioral relevance or learned valence of the sounds.
source: Furthermore, it suggests that increased encoding efficiency resulting from decreased spiking is a general effect of auditory attention in deep-layer BS units, regardless of the context-based behavioral relevance or learned valence of the sounds.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the consistency of encoding efficiency changes across stimulus types.

claim: Units with increased FRs (39%; n=96) exhibited a significant increase in A-rule decoding accuracy.
source: We found that units with increased FRs (39%; n=96) exhibited a significant increase in A-rule decoding accuracy (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C; p=0.0030, Z=–2.97, med. FC: 1.04, V-rule % correct: 66.4±15.5, A-rule: 69.5±15.5, n=96; paired WSR; FC: A-rule/V-rule; mean ± SDs), but no significant change in encoding efficiency (p=0.84, Z=0.2, V-rule bits/spike: 0.18±0.15, A-rule: 0.18±0.16).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the FR+ subpopulation.

claim: Units with suppressed FRs (60%; n=146) showed no significant change in decoding accuracy but a 44% increase in encoding efficiency.
source: By contrast, units with suppressed FRs (60%; n=146) showed no significant change in decoding accuracy (Figure 7—figure supplement 3D; p=0.44, Z=0.77, V-rule: 67.32±15.25, A-rule: 66.53±14.61), but a 44% increase in encoding efficiency (p=1.8e-07, Z=–5.22, median FC: 1.44, V-rule: 0.13±0.12, A-rule: 0.18±0.19; paired WSR).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the FR- subpopulation.

claim: The minority of units that increase FRs in the A-rule perform marginally better at decoding the auditory stimulus, and the units that decrease FRs drive the shift in encoding efficiency.
source: These results suggest that the minority of units that increase FRs in the A-rule perform marginally better at decoding the auditory stimulus, and that the units that decrease FRs drive the shift in encoding efficiency.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the analysis of FR+ and FR- subpopulations.

claim: If attentional modulation is behaviorally meaningful, FRs preceding A-rule error trials may be more similar to sound-unattended V-rule trials than to A-rule correct trials.
source: We hypothesized that, if this attentional modulation is behaviorally meaningful, FRs preceding A-rule error trials may be more similar to sound-unattended V-rule trials than to A-rule correct trials.
evidence: The manuscript states a hypothesis to test the behavioral relevance of neural modulation.

claim: Deep cortical BS units with A-rule suppression showed significantly higher pre-stimulus FRs prior to A-rule FA trials than CR trials.
source: However, deep cortical BS units with A-rule suppression showed significantly higher pre-stimulus FRs prior to A-rule FA trials than CR trials (deep BS [n=98]: mean FR difference between pre-stimulus FA and CR trials = 0.35 Hz, p=0.0098, Z=–3.15; paired WSR; other depth groups: p≥0.28, |Z|≤1.48; all p-values FDR-adjusted).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing pre-stimulus FRs across trial outcomes.

claim: Pre-stimulus FRs in A-rule-suppressed or A-rule-enhanced units did not differ between FA and CR trials in the V-rule.
source: This is unlikely to reflect a motor effect of higher FR before a lick, as it was specific to the A-rule: pre-stimulus FRs in A-rule-suppressed or A-rule-enhanced units did not differ between FA and CR trials in the V-rule (Figure 8C.c; Figure 8—source data 1B; paired WSR: all p≥0.68, all |Z|≤1.59, FDR-adjusted p-values).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis ruling out a motor-related explanation.

claim: FR reductions typical of modality-selective attention directly relate to behavioral outcomes.
source: Together, these findings suggest that FR reductions typical of modality-selective attention directly relate to behavioral outcomes.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the relationship between pre-stimulus FRs and trial outcomes.

claim: Attending to sound elements in an AV stream reduced both pre-stimulus and stimulus-evoked spiking activity, primarily in deep-layer neurons and neurons without spectrotemporal tuning.
source: Attending to sound elements in an AV stream reduced both pre-stimulus and stimulus-evoked spiking activity, primarily in deep-layer neurons and neurons without spectrotemporal tuning.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Despite reduced spiking, stimulus decoder accuracy was preserved, suggesting improved sound encoding efficiency.
source: Despite reduced spiking, stimulus decoder accuracy was preserved, suggesting improved sound encoding efficiency.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Task-irrelevant mapping stimuli during inter-trial intervals evoked fewer spikes without impairing stimulus encoding, indicating that attentional modulation generalized beyond training stimuli.
source: Similarly, task-irrelevant mapping stimuli during inter-trial intervals evoked fewer spikes without impairing stimulus encoding, indicating that attentional modulation generalized beyond training stimuli.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Spiking reductions predicted trial-to-trial behavioral accuracy during auditory attention, but not visual attention.
source: Importantly, spiking reductions predicted trial-to-trial behavioral accuracy during auditory attention, but not visual attention.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Auditory attention facilitates sound discrimination by filtering sound-irrelevant background activity in AC.
source: Together, these findings suggest auditory attention facilitates sound discrimination by filtering sound-irrelevant background activity in AC, and that the deepest cortical layers serve as a hub for integrating extramodal contextual information.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The deepest cortical layers serve as a hub for integrating extramodal contextual information.
source: Together, these findings suggest auditory attention facilitates sound discrimination by filtering sound-irrelevant background activity in AC, and that the deepest cortical layers serve as a hub for integrating extramodal contextual information.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Attentional selection operates cooperatively at many levels of sensory processing.
source: Attentional selection operates cooperatively at many levels of sensory processing.
evidence: The manuscript states established knowledge about attention.

claim: Most effort has been devoted to understanding the neural mechanisms of feature-selective attention within a single modality.
source: Most effort has been devoted to understanding the neural mechanisms of feature-selective attention within a single modality (Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Fritz et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on feature-selective attention.

claim: Attention to a stimulus feature or space will often increase stimulus-evoked spiking responses and reduce thresholds for eliciting a response.
